articles.title: Four Words at the Top of the Page
articles.dek: James walks in on a room of merchants planning their profits and asks them one question about fog. His answer gives every plan we make a better place to stand.
articles.quote: Because life is a mist, the good you already know to do belongs to today.
articles.body:
At five o'clock on a November morning in La Trinidad, Benguet, the hamog comes down off the mountains so thick that a farmer standing at the edge of his strawberry field cannot see the end of his own rows. Picture one of those farmers, and call him Mang Ramon. He has worked these slopes for thirty years, and he sits on an upturned crate with a thermos of barako and a small spiral notebook gone soft at the corners. In pencil he writes out the season: when to lay the plastic mulch, how many runners to transplant, which buyer from Manila to call before Christmas, and how much he hopes to set aside for his granddaughter's tuition.

At the top of every page, before any of the numbers, he writes four words in a careful hand: Kung loloobin ng Diyos. If God wills it. His children tease him about it, because the phrase is so common in Filipino mouths that most of us say it the way we say po, out of habit and good manners. Mang Ramon writes it on purpose, every single page. By eight o'clock the fog has burned away and the whole valley lies open in the sun, every row of red fruit visible at once, so he closes the notebook and goes to work.

The apostle James would have understood that farmer completely. James was the brother of Jesus and the steady leader of the church in Jerusalem, and he wrote this short, practical letter to "the twelve tribes scattered among the nations" (James 1:1), Jewish believers spread across the Roman world. Many of them made their living by trade, moving cloth, oil, spices and pottery along the roads and sea lanes between cities like Antioch, Ephesus and Alexandria. Near the end of chapter 4, James paints a scene that any of his readers would have recognized from their own dinner tables.

Imagine a lamplit room in a busy port city. A few men lean over a table, and one of them taps his finger on a spot on the map. They will leave tomorrow, or perhaps the day after, once the cargo is loaded. They will rent a stall in the new city, stay a full year, buy low and sell high, and come home with their purses heavy. The wine is poured, the plan is sealed, and everyone is smiling. Then James steps through the doorway as if he has been listening the whole time: "Now listen, you who say, 'Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business and make money.' Why, you do not even know what will happen tomorrow" (James 4:13–14).

The room goes quiet. Then James asks the question that has followed his readers for two thousand years, and he answers it before anyone can speak.

"What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes. Instead, you ought to say, 'If it is the Lord's will, we will live and do this or that.'" (James 4:14–15)

The Greek word James chooses for mist is atmis, which means vapor, steam or smoke. Luke uses the same word in Acts 2:19 for "billows of smoke." A Filipino reader can picture it easily, because it is the puff of steam that rises when you lift the lid off the rice pot in the morning. It is real, it is warm, it fills the kitchen with a good smell for a moment, and then it is gone into the air. James is gentle here. He is reminding hardworking people of something the wise have always known, as Proverbs 27:1 puts it: "Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring."

What surprises me most is how much of the merchants' plan James lets stand. He leaves every detail on the table: the travel, the year away, the business and even the profit. Commerce is honest work, and James never calls it otherwise. What concerns him is the one name missing from the whole conversation. The plan was drawn up as though the planners held tomorrow in their own hands, and in verse 16 James gives that attitude a name: "As it is, you boast in your arrogant schemes." The word behind "arrogant" is alazoneia. In Greek comedy, the alazon was a stock character, the swaggering boaster who promised what he could never deliver. The apostle John uses the same word for "the pride of life" (1 John 2:16).

Then comes the remedy, and it is wonderfully simple. "If it is the Lord's will, we will live and do this or that." James places even the act of living inside that little phrase, since every breath tomorrow is a gift we have not yet received. Yet the sentence still ends with "do this or that." The plans survive. James hands the notebook back to the merchants and invites them to keep writing, only now with God's name written above the numbers. The early church took this seriously. When Paul left Ephesus, "he promised, 'I will come back if it is God's will'" (Acts 18:21), and he told the Corinthians, "I will come to you very soon, if the Lord is willing" (1 Corinthians 4:19). The greatest missionary of his age kept a full calendar, and he held it in open hands.

Then James adds one more sentence, and it changes the direction of the whole passage. After talking about mist and uncertainty, a reader might expect him to say, "So take it easy, hold everything loosely, and wait to see what happens." Instead he writes: "If anyone, then, knows the good they ought to do and doesn't do it, it is sin for them" (James 4:17). That small word "then" ties the verse to everything before it. The shortness of life becomes the reason to act, and to act today. Because life is a mist, the good you already know to do belongs to today.

This is where James speaks so clearly to us as Filipinos. We have a phrase, bahala na, that can carry two very different hearts. On a good day it is courage, the faith of someone who steps forward and trusts God with the outcome. On a tired day it can become a way to postpone, a quiet hope that someone or something else will handle what we already know is ours to do. James honors the first and gently closes the door on the second. Humble trust in God's will always comes with willing hands.

So the next time you plan your week, whether it is a business proposal, a move abroad, a wedding budget or just the list of errands on your phone, try writing Mang Ramon's four words at the top: Kung loloobin ng Diyos. Let them do their work on your heart, reminding you that tomorrow is a gift. Then look at your list and ask which good thing you have been carrying around for weeks, perhaps the apology to a brother, the call to a lola in the province, or the small debt you meant to settle. Do that one today, while the morning is still yours.

None of this is meant to frighten you. Earlier in this same chapter James promises that God "gives us more grace" (James 4:6) and that if we "come near to God," he "will come near to you" (James 4:8). The God who numbers our days also walks beside us inside them. A mist may last only a little while, but in La Trinidad the lifting of the fog is the moment the whole field comes into view. May your plans today be written under his name, and may the good you do before the sun is high be the harvest he was hoping to see.

articles.title: The Ship Built From Borrowed Planks
articles.dek: Ezekiel's lament over Tyre lists every nation that helped build the city's glory. Tyre's pride began on the day it forgot that list.
articles.quote: Every beautiful thing in your life was carried to you by someone else's hands, and gratitude is simply remembering their names.
articles.body:
On December 23, 1783, a tall Virginian in a plain coat walked into the Maryland State House in Annapolis, where the Continental Congress was meeting. George Washington had just won a war that very few people had expected him to win. The army loved him, much of the young country adored him, and more than a few people assumed he would now rule. History was full of victorious generals who turned their swords into crowns, and Washington had the soldiers, the fame, and the timing to do the same.

He read a short speech instead, and the paper shook in his hand. He thanked the officers who had served beside him and commended the nation "to the protection of Almighty God." Then he said, "Having now finished the work assigned me, I retire from the great theatre of Action," and he handed his commission back to the civilian government that had given it to him. By Christmas Eve he was home at Mount Vernon. The painter Benjamin West later recalled that when King George III heard that Washington meant to give up power, the king said that if he did, he would be the greatest man in the world.

The moment is moving because of the way Washington understood his own success. In his letters and speeches he kept pointing away from himself. He pointed to the soldiers who had gone hungry through the Valley Forge winter, to the officers he named aloud, and to a Providence he believed had carried them all. He seemed to know that his victory was built from other people's courage. That knowledge kept him humble enough to walk away from a crown, and it is exactly what the ancient city of Tyre lost.

Ezekiel was a priest living among the Jewish exiles in Babylon around 586 BC, the year Jerusalem fell. Tyre, the great Phoenician port on the coast of what is now Lebanon, heard the news and gloated: "Aha! The gate to the nations is broken" (Ezekiel 26:2). Part of the city stood on a rocky island just off the shore, guarded by water and high walls, and it had grown rich as the shipping hub of the Mediterranean. Its merchants sold the famous purple dye that only royalty could afford. To anyone living then, Tyre looked unsinkable.

So God gave Ezekiel a lament, a funeral song, to sing before the funeral had even happened. In chapter 27 the prophet pictures Tyre as a magnificent merchant ship. "You say, Tyre, 'I am perfect in beauty'" (Ezekiel 27:3). Then he walks us through the shipyard. The planks are juniper from Senir and the mast is a cedar from Lebanon. The oars are oak from Bashan, the deck is inlaid with ivory from Cyprus, and the sail is embroidered linen from Egypt (27:5–7). The rowers come from Sidon and Arvad, and veteran craftsmen from Byblos caulk the seams (27:8–9).

After the ship comes the marketplace. The chapter opens into one of the longest trade lists in the Bible. Tarshish brings silver, iron, tin, and lead. Greece trades in slaves and bronze. Judah and Israel send wheat, honey, olive oil, and balm. Damascus brings wine, Arabia brings lambs and goats, and Sheba brings spices and gold (27:12–22). A modern reader may find the list tedious, but its length is deliberate. Tyre's glory was put together from dozens of peoples, and each of them supplied a plank. Then, in a single verse, the wind changes: "Your oarsmen take you out to the high seas. But the east wind will break you to pieces in the heart of the sea" (27:26). Every cargo that was listed so lovingly sinks with her, and the sailors of the world stand on the shore and wail.

Chapter 28 explains why. God speaks directly to the ruler of Tyre and names the exact place where the ship began to take on water:

"By your great skill in trading you have increased your wealth, and because of your wealth your heart has grown proud." (Ezekiel 28:5)

The Hebrew verb behind "grown proud" is gabah, which means to be high or lifted up. It is the word you would use for a tall cedar or a towering mountain, so a literal rendering might be that Tyre's heart grew tall. The verse does not condemn skill, trade, or wealth. God even credits the king with real wisdom and understanding (28:4). The trouble started when his heart rose above everything that held it up. A few verses earlier the king says, "I am a god; I sit on the throne of a god in the heart of the seas," and God answers, "But you are a mere mortal and not a god" (28:2).

Read chapters 27 and 28 side by side and a quiet irony appears. Tyre boasted, "I am perfect in beauty," but the chapter before has just shown us that its beauty was borrowed, plank by plank, from Lebanon, Egypt, Cyprus, and Judah. The cedar came from the mountains, the linen was woven by Egyptian hands, and the strength in the oars belonged to the men of Sidon. One way to read this lament is that pride is a kind of forgetting. Tyre stopped seeing the hands that had built it and came to believe it had made itself. God later says, "Your heart became proud on account of your beauty, and you corrupted your wisdom because of your splendor" (28:17). Pride had even spoiled its wisdom, because people who forget where they came from soon misjudge where they are going.

Verses 12 to 19 move into grander language still. They picture the king as one who was placed in Eden, covered in precious stones, and then cast down. Many Christians through the centuries have heard in these lines an echo of the fall of Satan, while others read them as poetry about a human king. On either reading the pattern holds: a creature given every good gift decided the gifts were his own. History kept Ezekiel's word. Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years, and in 332 BC Alexander the Great built a causeway out to the island and took the city. Centuries later, Revelation 18 borrowed Ezekiel's lament, with the merchants weeping over their lost cargoes, to describe the fall of every proud empire.

The apostle Paul put the remedy into a single question: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?" (1 Corinthians 4:7). In the Bible's view, humility is largely gratitude with a good memory. It lets us enjoy our gifts without being ruled by them, because we keep remembering who gave them.

Filipinos have a phrase for that kind of memory: utang na loob, the debt of the inner self that we owe to those who helped us. At its best it is exactly what Tyre lacked. It is the nurse in Riyadh who still remembers the tita who paid her board exam fee, and the engineer who still visits the barrio teacher who stayed late to help him with fractions. Our lives are ships too, and if we look closely, every plank came from somewhere. One came from a mother's sacrifice and another from a friend's loan. Others came from a mentor's patience, a church that prayed for us by name, and a God who gives us every breath.

Success has a way of erasing that list. The more we achieve, the easier it becomes to tell our story with ourselves at the center, until one day we hear ourselves say, in some small way, "I am perfect in beauty." Tonight, you might take a sheet of paper and write your own ship's manifest, naming the people who supplied the timber, the sail, and the oars of the life you have now. Then choose one name from the list and reach out today, with a text, a phone call, or a visit, to say thank you plainly.

Washington could hand back his commission because he knew it had never fully belonged to him, and that knowledge set him free. The same freedom is open to you. Every beautiful thing in your life was carried to you by someone else's hands, and gratitude is simply remembering their names. Behind all those hands stands the first Giver, for "every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights" (James 1:17). A heart that remembers this can sail through success and storm alike, because it knows whose it is.

articles.title: Treasure in the Dark Cave
articles.dek: A persecuted poet says God's word makes him feel like a soldier gathering plunder. In the same stanza he names what that plunder turns out to be.
articles.quote: The heart that has learned to tremble at God's word slowly stops trembling at everything else.
articles.body:
Sometime in the winter of 1946 or early 1947 (the accounts differ on the exact date), a young Bedouin shepherd named Muhammed edh-Dhib was climbing the cliffs above the northwestern shore of the Dead Sea, looking for a goat that had wandered off. It is a bare, bleached country of crumbling limestone and hot wind, and the caves in those cliffs are small dark openings in the rock. In the story he told later, he tossed a stone into one of them, hoping to scare the animal out. Instead of a bleat, he heard the sound of pottery breaking.

When he and his cousins crawled inside, they found tall clay jars, and inside some of the jars were bundles of old leather wrapped in linen. The boys had no idea what they were holding. The bundles were sold to a dealer in Bethlehem for a modest sum, passed from hand to hand, and finally reached scholars who unrolled them with very careful fingers. One of them was a complete scroll of the prophet Isaiah, more than seven metres long, copied over a century before Jesus was born. It was about a thousand years older than any complete Hebrew copy of Isaiah known at the time. When scholars laid it beside the Bible they already had, they found the words had been carried across those ten centuries with remarkable faithfulness. A boy looking for a lost goat had found one of the great treasures of the twentieth century.

A few years later, in another cave nearby, a large scroll of the Psalms came to light. Among its columns are lines from Psalm 119, including part of the very stanza we read today. For two thousand years, in the dark, a scribe's patient handwriting had been holding a sentence about the joy of finding treasure.

Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, and it is built with great care. It is an acrostic, a poem arranged by the alphabet: twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every one of the eight lines in a stanza begins with that stanza's letter. Today's section is the second to last, the stanza of the letter shin. We do not know for certain who wrote it, but the writer tells us a good deal about his life. He is a man under pressure from powerful people. Early in the psalm he says, "Though rulers sit together and slander me, your servant will meditate on your decrees" (Psalm 119:23). By this late stanza those same rulers are still at it, and he opens with them.

"Rulers persecute me without cause, but my heart trembles at your word. I rejoice in your promise like one who finds great spoil." (Psalm 119:161–162)

The word translated "spoil" is the Hebrew shalal, and it has a very specific meaning. It is plunder, the goods gathered from the field after a battle: the gold, the cloth, the livestock that the winning army carries home. Isaiah uses the same picture when he describes God's people rejoicing "as warriors rejoice when dividing the plunder" (Isaiah 9:3). Spoil belongs to people who have won.

That makes the psalmist's choice of image surprising. By every outward measure he is on the losing side. The people with power are hunting him, and he has done nothing to deserve it, which is what "without cause" means. Yet when he opens God's promise, he speaks like a soldier walking a battlefield after the victory, bending down to pick up treasures he did not forge and could never have afforded. One way to read this is that the psalmist understands whose battle it really is. The rulers can take a great deal from him, but in God's word he keeps finding riches that no one handed him and no one can confiscate. He also says he is one who finds it. The Hebrew verb carries the gladness of discovery, the feeling of a shepherd boy hearing a jar break in the dark.

The first line matters too. "My heart trembles at your word" uses a Hebrew word for awe and dread. The psalmist has a healthy fear, and he has pointed it at the right place. Powerful people are real, but they are smaller than the voice of God, and a heart that stands in reverent awe before that voice finds its other fears shrinking to their proper size. The heart that has learned to tremble at God's word slowly stops trembling at everything else.

Then, three lines later, the stanza tells us what the treasure turns out to be. In Hebrew, verse 162 speaks of shalal rav, "great spoil." Verse 165 answers with shalom rav, "great peace": "Great peace have those who love your law, and nothing can make them stumble" (Psalm 119:165). The two phrases sound almost alike, both begin with this stanza's letter, and both are called "great." This suggests the poet wants us to hear them together. The plunder he carries home from God's word is peace, a deep settledness that the rulers outside cannot reach. The word for "stumble" refers to an obstacle in the path, something that trips the feet. A person can still be surrounded by obstacles and keep walking, because their footing rests on something firmer than their circumstances.

Jesus told a story in the same spirit: "The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. When a man found it, he hid it again, and then in his joy went and sold all he had and bought that field" (Matthew 13:44). In both places the joy comes first, and the obedience flows out of it. The psalmist says it plainly near the end of the stanza: "I obey your statutes, for I love them greatly" (Psalm 119:167). Love for God's word comes before the obedience, as its source.

Many of us know the rulers of this psalm in smaller forms. They may be a supervisor who takes credit for your work, a relative whose words at every family gathering leave you feeling small, or an office where you need a signature and keep being sent back to the end of the line. You did nothing to deserve it, and still it comes. In those seasons, opening the Bible can feel like holding a bundle of dry leather, words you have seen many times that seem to have nothing to do with Monday.

The psalmist invites us to read as finders. He came to the word expecting to discover something, and he did, again and again, which is why he could say, "Seven times a day I praise you for your righteous laws" (Psalm 119:164). Seven in Scripture often stands for fullness, so the line pictures a whole day returning to God. You could practice this in a very simple way today. Read these eight verses slowly, choose the one line that catches your heart, and write it on a small piece of paper or set it on your phone, then come back to it whenever the pressure rises, on the jeepney, at your desk, or before you answer that difficult message.

Muhammed edh-Dhib went into the cliffs looking for a goat, and he came out carrying something the whole world would treasure. Many of us open the Bible looking for something small, a little comfort or a few minutes of quiet before the day begins. God is generous with people who come that way. The psalmist adds a last line of comfort: "All my ways are known to you" (Psalm 119:168). The One who sees every unfair thing done to you is the same One who has hidden treasure in his word for you to find, and the peace you carry out of it today is yours to keep.

articles.title: The Rice That Stands Back Up
articles.dek: Proverbs 24 admits that good people fall again and again. Then it tells us why they keep rising, and how to treat others when they go down.
articles.quote: The righteous fall as often as anyone; what marks them is the hand that keeps lifting them back up.
articles.body:
After a strong typhoon crosses Central Luzon, the photographs from the rice fields look like defeat. Whole paddies lie flattened, the green stalks pressed sideways into the mud as if a giant palm had smoothed them down. Farmers call this lodging, and it is one of the most discouraging sights a planter can see in the weeks before harvest. Yet if the stems have bent without snapping, something remarkable begins to happen in the days after the wind dies down.

Rice, like wheat and the other grasses, has small swollen joints along its stem called nodes. At each joint sits a little cushion of living tissue that botanists call a pulvinus, and its cells can sense which way is down. When a stalk is knocked flat, the cells on the underside of the joint start to grow longer while the cells on the upper side stay as they are. That uneven growth bends the stem at the knee and slowly lifts the head of grain back toward the sky. Over several days a field that looked finished can rise visibly, the stalks crooked at the joints but pointing upward again. The plant was made from the beginning with the expectation that it would be knocked down, and with the means to stand back up.

Nearly three thousand years ago, a group of Hebrew teachers said much the same thing about the people of God. Our passage sits near the end of a section that Proverbs itself calls "the sayings of the wise" (Proverbs 22:17), a collection of "thirty sayings" (Proverbs 22:20) gathered to train young people for a life of responsibility and integrity. Many scholars note that the opening part of this collection echoes an older Egyptian teaching text, which reminds us that Israel's wise men knew the wider world well. What they added was the conviction that the God of Israel stands behind every outcome.

The passage opens by speaking to a would-be predator. "Do not lurk like a thief near the house of the righteous, do not plunder their dwelling place" (Proverbs 24:15). Picture a man in a small village watching his neighbor's house, noting when the family leaves for the fields and when the gate is left unlatched, quietly calculating what he could take. The teacher's first argument to him is a practical one. Leave that family alone, because they possess a resilience you cannot see, and every scheme you aim at them will fail in the end. Then comes the reason, one of the most hopeful sentences in the whole book.

"For though the righteous fall seven times, they rise again, but the wicked stumble when calamity strikes." (Proverbs 24:16)

The first surprise is how honest this verse is. It simply assumes that the righteous fall. In Hebrew thought, seven is the number of fullness and completion, so "seven times" means over and over, as often as life can knock a person down. The word for fall, naphal, is the ordinary Hebrew word for a collapse, used elsewhere of city walls coming down and of soldiers dropping in battle. Proverbs is describing real failures, real losses, and real seasons face-down in the mud. The good person in this verse is defined by what happens next: "they rise again." The verb there, qum, is the plain word for getting up off the ground, and it carries the sense of being set upright and established.

The second surprise comes in the other half of the verse. The wicked "stumble when calamity strikes," and the sentence ends there, with no rising at all. The difference between the two people lies in what holds them up. A companion psalm says it beautifully: "The LORD makes firm the steps of the one who delights in him; though he may stumble, he will not fall, for the LORD upholds him with his hand" (Psalm 37:23–24). Like the pulvinus hidden in the joint of a rice stalk, the power to rise is something God has placed inside the life of his people. It works quietly, often slowly, and usually leaves us a little crooked at the knees, yet it turns us back toward the light.

The gospel takes this proverb further than its first readers could have imagined. In the New Testament, the righteous are those whom God has declared right through faith in Jesus, which means our standing rests on his grace rather than on our track record. Peter is the clearest picture. He fell as hard as a disciple can fall, denying his Lord three times on the night Jesus most needed a friend. After the resurrection, Jesus met him on a beach and asked him three times, "Do you love me?" (John 21:15–17), restoring him once for every denial. Peter rose again because Someone came down to the shore and lifted him. The prophet Micah had spoken the same hope centuries before: "Though I have fallen, I will rise. Though I sit in darkness, the LORD will be my light" (Micah 7:8).

Then the passage makes a turn that catches many readers off guard. Having warned the predator to leave the righteous alone, the teacher now speaks to the righteous themselves: "Do not gloat when your enemy falls; when they stumble, do not let your heart rejoice, or the LORD will see and disapprove and turn his wrath away from them" (Proverbs 24:17–18). The reasoning can sound strange at first, as though the point were to keep the enemy's punishment on schedule. One way to read it is that God cares deeply about the heart of the person watching. Gloating places you on the same ground as the one who fell, and God takes that more seriously than your enemy's mistakes. A person who has fallen seven times and been raised by grace has no reason to celebrate someone else lying in the mud. Jesus showed this on the cross when he prayed for the very men driving the nails, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34).

These two halves of the passage belong together, and they meet in ordinary Filipino life. Maybe you are the one who has fallen again. It might be the board exam you failed for the second time, the temper you promised your family you had conquered, or the small business that closed after you poured your savings into it. Proverbs does not shame you for being on the ground. It reminds you that falling is part of the story of every righteous person, and that the Lord who upholds you is already at work in the joint where you bent. Your next step can be small and faithful, like opening the reviewer again tomorrow morning, asking your spouse for forgiveness tonight, or calling the friend who believed in you to tell them honestly where you are.

Or maybe someone else has fallen, and you feel the old pull to enjoy it. A former boss is in the news for the wrong reasons, a classmate who once mocked you has lost everything, or a screenshot about someone you dislike is going around the group chat. The pull to forward it, to add a laughing reaction, or to say "buti nga" is very human. A better habit is to pray for that person by name before you say anything about them at all, asking God to do for them what he has done for you so many times.

Rice farmers who have lived through many typhoons learn not to declare a field lost on the morning after the storm. They wait a few days and watch the stalks begin to lift. God is far more patient with his people than any farmer with his crop. The righteous fall as often as anyone; what marks them is the hand that keeps lifting them back up. Whatever flattened you this week, stay rooted, turn your face toward him, and trust that the rising has already begun.
